header.title: Sermones inediti: AI translation (Claude)
header.author: SS Leo I. Magnus
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's tmp907.tmp907.opp-lat1, from Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. The whole work is translated. It was chosen because no English translation of it could be found.
header.statement: An AI-generated translation of the whole work, checked against the original by a second AI only in samples. No specialist has reviewed it.
header.availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

Many scanning errors corrected silently (e.g. 'III' read as 'ut', 'sngaciia i' as 'sagacitati', 'eassate' as 'cassate', 'reguum' as 'regnum'). In Sermon I, 'de i iarum in victu viia' is damaged; read as 'deliciarum in victu vita' (by luxuries in diet life). 'De Pallia' in the heading of Sermon III is evidently 'De Pascha', as the content shows. Sermon III closely follows Melito of Sardis, On the Pasch. In Sermon II, the final 'Nisi ipse...' sentence lacks a main clause in the Latin; the bracketed supplement in the English supplies one. 'Pasce jejunum' may mean 'feed the hungry' rather than 'the fasting'.

Line 10: 'ut tuus Filius patiamur' is evidently corrupt for 'patiatur'; so translated. The scriptural references as printed (Jer. 22:5, Acts 17:5) do not match the standard verses (Jer. 22:3; Acts 17:3). Line 11: 'concinam' read as 'coronam'. Line 14: 'q. lect.' is abbreviated or damaged, taken as 'in the reading'; 'ascenderit' taken as 'descenderit', as the sense requires. Line 15: 'Delium' taken as 'fletuum' (of weeping); 'remissi, num' as 'remissionum'. Line 17: 'quam totam accelerare' is unclear, rendered by sense as 'whom it befits to make haste'.

Line 18: 'dediticulis' is evidently corrupt; rendered as 'petty worldly pleasures', perhaps reading 'delectatiunculis'. Line 19: 'tremens' may be a misreading of 'fremens' (raging). Sermon VI corresponds to the Latin version of Proclus of Constantinople's first homily on the Theotokos, not a work of Leo. In it, 'naturae rubus, quem divini partus ignis combussit' literally says the fire 'burned' the bush; the sense, drawn from Exodus, is that the fire did not consume it. The interpretation of Gabriel is garbled: the parenthetical '(filius)' is editorial, and the intended sense is that the name means 'God and man'. 'radius' is taken as the weaver's shuttle. 'scientia corporis (sic)' is marked corrupt by the editor; I translated it literally. 'te duxerat' is obscure and may be corrupt.

First line: 'Hominis igitur pueri' read as 'hominis puri' (a mere man). 'Diabolus ei mortem exportabat in magno periculo' is obscure and possibly corrupt. 'Quomodo ergo poterat utraque homo purus salvare' is garbled; rendered as 'do both'. 'Quod emerat salvavit' may be a corruption of 'quod erat salvavit' (by what he was he saved). 'Seraphim non proficiebant' may stand for 'non prospiciebant' (could not look upon [him]). 'Erutis' read as 'eratis'. Ezekiel 'ad piam portae' read as 'ad viam portae'. Sermon VII: 'Diona insula' is unidentified.

'Astices' read as 'apices' (letters). 'Aristarcus' (scholar/critic, perhaps a title) and 'primicerius' kept. Symmachus, Apollinaris the Chronopagite, Minander, the Sichaean gate, 'Popedon' (for Poseidon) and 'Apollinis' as a personal name are as the text gives them; the topography is legendary and largely unidentifiable. 'Argolicae artis' (the Argolic art) is unclear, perhaps Greek learning. In VII Dionysius answers alone but the verb 'dixerunt' is plural; kept. 'De Thessalonica convertens' is odd but translated as given. The psalm reference in VIII is to Christ's healing (John 9:6).

Several scanning errors are read as evident: in XI 'cere ... ombierunt, < i quasi es' as 'ecce ... ambierunt, et quasi ex', and '< opia' as 'copia'. In Sermon VIII.2 'fratris in funi' is unclear; it is taken as 'on him [Absalom]' for the murder of his brother (Amnon). In VIII.3 'parentur filio' is read as 'parcatur filio', 'sui sanguinem' as 'sitit sanguinem', and 'ocucta' as 'cuncta'. In VIII.2 'pietatis fra ura' is read as 'pietatis natura'.

Line 37: 'a sali (sic) subducto' is corrupt as printed; rendered as the mount (the mule) being drawn from under him, which the context requires. Line 38: 'etiam netur host s interitus' is damaged; read as 'etiam fletur hostis interitus' ('the enemy's death is even wept for'). 'Quasi Absalom quod ausus est comprobaris' is awkward; taken as 'you seem to approve what Absalom dared'. Scanning errors silently corrected include nudivil/audivit, I gna/ligna, læsi panis/læsi patris, defensa cat/defensa est.

nodes.text: UNPUBLISHED SERMONS OF SAINT LEO THE GREAT, drawn from the libraries of Florence, edited by A. B. Caillau, priest of the Society of Mercy, together with Doctor Saint-Yves of the same Society.
NOTICE.

Of these sermons, all of which bear the name of Saint Leo the pope in the manuscripts, some seem rightly attributable to him, and others plainly depart from his manner of speaking. But so that we may not be reproached with a certain boldness, as happened with our edition of Saint Augustine, when some suspected that we had wished to impose our opinion on everyone, we set these discourses before the eyes of readers just as they stand in the manuscripts, leaving this part of the work to their discernment, so that each may separate by his own judgement what is genuine from what is spurious.
FIRST SERMON.
On the time of fasting.

I. Most beloved, your faith prompts us to set out the teachings of religion. For we exhort [you] to fasting, which is for those who live rightly an increase of devotion, a wall of faith, the overthrow of wickedness. We urge too that one must always abstain not only from foods but from all vices. Do not be prodigal in revelling or arrogant in drunkenness; for it is written in Solomon: The body which is corrupted weighs down the soul (Wis. 9:15). And the Apostle also says: Make no provision for the flesh in your desires (Rom. 13:14). Abstain therefore in these days from worldly cares and carnal desires. Let the body be chastised, so that the soul may be filled. For the spirit is strengthened when the flesh is thinned by frugality. For by luxuries in diet the present life is nourished, not the future one, since luxury accompanies abundance of goods. Put away from you envies, quarrels, evil speaking, contentions, and break up all the seeds of sins. Make void the snares of violent actions and the knotted arguments of false accusations. Provide lodging for the needy and for those of the household of faith. Tear up unjust bonds of debt, so that you may keep fasts pleasing to God not only in body but also in spirit.

II. We must also hope for the fruits of our own fasting from the seed of almsgiving. For it is written: As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin (Ecclus. 3:33). We must also act so that we are seen to abstain from rich fare not out of zeal for avarice but out of concern for mercy. Let us give temporal things to the poor, so that everlasting rewards may be granted to us through their prayers. For by the exchange of a little bread and copper, freedom from punishment for sins is conferred on us. We should know also that the Lord made many poor, just as [he made] many infirm, so that there might be a need to entreat the Lord, and that you who have suffered none of these things may fear lest perhaps you suffer them. Feed, then, you who are healthy, the infirm man, as an example of a calamity [borne] in your stead. Feed, then, you rich man, the poor man, whose portion perhaps you received from the Lord our God so that you might feed him. Feed the fasting, lest his share be taken from you and given to another who will bestow it. Feed the one dying of hunger; for whoever could have saved a man by feeding him, if he has not fed him, has killed him.

III. Let the desires of beggars who keep silent also be anticipated, since we read: Blessed is he who considers the needy and the poor; the Lord will deliver him in the evil day (Ps. 40:2). Let us therefore give food to the needy before they ask, lest, crying out from excessive need, they seem to be pressing us as we delay. Let us offer them at least some portion of the heavenly gifts bestowed on us, lest for our sloth we repay penal interest to our creditor. Let us think of that rich man who, on account of crumbs of bread, asked for a drop of water and did not receive it. Let us recall that widow who, by putting two coppers into the treasury, offered to God the whole living that she had. Let us too give to our brothers at least what is left over to us. Nor indeed ought we to carry out the divine commands sad and as hypocrites, but let us give thanks to God, the author of our generosity, so that, praying constantly, we may supply the needy with the substance of temporal life, that we may attain eternal life, by the gift of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.
SERMON II.
On the Passion of the Lord.

I. After that first and universal ruin of human transgression, from which through one man sin entered into this world, and through sin death (Rom. 5:12), no one any longer could escape the dominion of the devil, no one the chains of dire captivity, nor would reconciliation to pardon or return to life lie open to anyone, unless God the Son, co-eternal and in all things co-equal with God the Father, deigned to become also the son of man, and to be hung bodily on the cross for the redemption and salvation of all men. For this was the cause of the redemption and salvation of the whole human race: that God himself in man truly suffered, and truly died, and truly rose from the dead, so that he might truly open the gates of the heavenly kingdom to men who believe in him and who die in his will, and redeem us from eternal death and punishment. For he bore many and various injuries for us, not because his own faults required it, he who never committed any sin, but solely because of our need; since we were chained with such hard chains, and rolled down into so deep an abyss of death, that we could not be set free except through his immense mercy, and through his human passion and death. [We could not have been freed] unless he himself redeemed [us] with his precious blood, unless he himself by his death took eternal punishments away from us, unless he himself broke the strength of the devil and led [us] with him to the heavenly kingdom, and granted to all of us who wish to remain in his will a sweet and easy road to the heavenly kingdom.

II. Therefore, dearest brothers, what must we do for such great benefits of God, except die to the world and its lusts, mortifying in ourselves carnal desires by vigils, by fasts, by chastity, by endurance of adversity, by perseverance in all goodness, and continually commend ourselves to God in prayers, redeeming ourselves from eternal punishments by repenting, weeping for and confessing our sins, and by alms; so that, upheld thus by divine help, we may deserve to remain in eternal blessedness there whither the merciful Lord our God has brought us back by his death, by the gift of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen.
SERMON III.
On the Pasch.

I. You have heard, most beloved brothers, the scripture of the Hebrew exodus and the words of the mystery: how the Lamb was sacrificed, how the people was saved, and how Pharaoh was struck through the mystery. Understand, most beloved, how the mystery of the Pasch is new and old, temporal and eternal, corruptible and incorrupt, mortal and immortal. Old according to the law, but new according to the Word; temporal through the type, eternal through the glory; corruptible because of the sacrifice of the beast, incorruptible because of the life of the Lord; mortal because of the burial, immortal because of the resurrection. The law indeed is old, but the word is new. The type is temporal, but the grace is everlasting; the sheep are corruptible, the Lord incorruptible. For he was broken as a lamb, but raised up as God. For he was led as a sheep to the sacrifice, yet he was not a sheep; and as a lamb without voice (Isa. 53:7), yet he was not a lamb. For those things were done in figure; these are found in truth. For in place of the lamb the Lord came, and in place of the beast a man, and the man is Christ, in whom all things are contained. And Isaiah says: As a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and as a lamb before the shearer, without voice, so he did not open his mouth. In humiliation his judgement was taken away. But who will declare his generation? (ibid. 7, 8). Many other things also were foretold by the prophets concerning the Pasch, the mystery of Jesus Christ, to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

II. For he, led as a lamb and slain as a sheep, redeemed us from the worship of the world as from Egypt, and saved us from the hand of the devil as from the hand of Pharaoh; and he sealed our souls with his own spirit, and the members of our body with his precious blood. This is he who clothed death with confusion and set the devil in mourning. This is he who struck down iniquity and injustice, as Moses condemned Egypt to barrenness. This is he who rescued us from slavery to freedom, from darkness to light, from death to life, from tyranny to an everlasting kingdom. This is he who endured many things in many; this is he who was slain in Abel, and bound by the feet in Isaac, and was a wanderer in Jacob, and was sold in Joseph, and was wrapped up in Moses, and exposed by his mother on the river, and slaughtered in the lamb, and persecuted in David, and dishonoured in the prophets. This is he who was buried in the earth and, rising from the dead, ascended to the heights of the heavens. This is the lamb without voice; this is he who was taken from the flock for the sacrifice, who was sacrificed at evening, who was buried at night. This is Jesus Christ our Lord, who rose from the dead and raised man from the grave below to life. This one, then, was slain in the midst of Jerusalem. By whom? By Israel. For what reason? Because he cured their lame, and cleansed the lepers, and gave light to the blind, and raised the dead.

III. What have you done, Israel, [this] so unheard-of injustice? You have dishonoured him who had made you honourable; you have shamed him who had glorified you; you have kept silent about him who had proclaimed you; you have killed him who had given you life. Is it not written: Do not shed innocent blood, lest you die most wretchedly (Jer. 22:5)? 'Therefore,' says Israel, 'I did this, because he had to suffer' (Acts 17:5). You are wrong, Israel, when you think in this way. He had to suffer, but not through you; he had to be subjected to insults, but not through you; he had to be hung on the gibbet of the cross, but it ought by no means to have been done by your right hand. With this cry, Israel, you ought to have called out to the Lord: 'O Lord, if your will has so decreed that your Son should suffer, yet let him by no means suffer through me. Let him rather be judged by foreigners; let him be nailed fast by the uncircumcised, by any tyrant you please. Far be it that this crime should be committed through me.' With this cry, Israel, you were by no means willing to call out, nor did you refrain from laying your own hands on your Lord. You did not stand in awe of his works; no shame struck you when the withered hand was restored sound to its own body, nor when closed eyes had been opened, nor when loosened limbs were made firm by his voice. Nor even did you blush at that recent miracle, when a man already four days dead rose from the tomb at the command of his voice.

IV. O Israel, you saw such great wonders of Christ, and you remained ever in unbelief. You indeed, passing over all these things, made ready for the death of the Lord. You prepared for him the sharpest nails, false witnesses, gall too, and the sword, as for a murderous robber. You also inflicted lashes on his poor body, and set a crown of thorns on his head, and bound with chains those good hands of his which had formed you from the soil; and that good mouth of his, through which you were fed with life, you fed in return with gall. On the great feast day you put your Lord to death. And you indeed were enjoying banquets, while he suffered the hunger of famine; you drank wine and ate bread, but he gall and vinegar; you were radiant in body, and he worn out with griefs; you exulted, and he was afflicted; you sang psalms, and he was being judged; you led dances, and he was being laid in the tomb; you indeed lay on soft couches, but he in a sepulchre and a coffin. O most impious Israel, why have you committed this unheard-of injustice? Subjecting your Lord to unheard-of sufferings you put him to death, your ruler, your maker, who honoured you, who gave you the name of Israel. But you were not found to be Israel, for you did not see the Lord, nor were you willing to understand God.

V. Did you not know, Israel, that this is the firstborn of God, who was begotten before the morning star? This is he who led you down into Egypt, and, preserving you there, supplied you with food. This is he who was sent to you, who cured your sick, who raised the dead. This is he against whom you acted wickedly, whom you slaughtered. This is he whom you sold. Therefore, Israel, because you did not tremble over the Lord, you trembled when assailed by enemies. Over the Lord you felt no dread; over the Lord you did not wail; over your dead sons you wailed. Because you abandoned the Lord, you will not be found by him; you dashed down the Lord, and you too will be dashed to the ground. And you indeed lie on the ground, but he, rising from the dead, has been carried up to the height of heaven.

VI. Now therefore come, all you families of men, who are mingled with sins, and receive the remission of sins. For the Lord says to you: For I am your remission, I the Pasch of salvation, I the lamb who was slaughtered for you; I your redemption, I life, I am your salvation, I your resurrection. I am your king, I will raise you up by my right hand. This is our Lord, who made heaven and earth; who was hung on the wood, who was buried in the earth, who rose from the dead, ascended to the heights of the heavens, and lives and reigns with the Father and with the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.
SERMON IV.
On the Pasch II.

I. Although all the solemnities, dearly beloved, which are celebrated in the Churches for the honour of God are holy and venerable, yet today's day of the Lord's resurrection has a festivity of its own. This is surely because all other days contain in themselves only the joy of the living, but this one also the gladness of the dead. This festivity, then, is shared alike by those below and those above, because the Lord, rising from the dead, gave a festival both there, where he conquered death, and here, where he returned as victor from death. And so the Psalmist rightly speaks of this day in particular, saying: This is the day which the Lord has made; let us exult and be glad in it (Ps. 117:24). For in announcing the Lord's resurrection he proclaimed a day of saving exultation not only to those above but to those below; because when the Lord descended into the dark gloom of the underworld, there too, without doubt, it was then a most brilliant day, where the Saviour shone forth. Hence the evangelist [says] beautifully in the reading: And that, he says, shines in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it (John 1:5); because although the Lord went down even into darkness, yet he did not feel the obscurity of the darkness. In that horror of night the light of eternal nature kept the inviolable splendour of his majesty, and thus the light was not overcome by the night, but the night by the light.

II. Let us rejoice, therefore, dearly beloved, and exult in the Lord. For today the light of salvation has been given to us by the Lord, according to what the same Psalmist says in what follows: The Lord is God, and he has shone upon us (Ps. 117:26). And what did he add further? Appoint, he says, a solemn day with crowded assemblies, even to the horn of the altar (ibid.). I see this too fulfilled today in the Church of God, for since everything up to the horn of the altar is full of devout gatherings, this fullness of the holy Church has fulfilled the Scripture. This day, then, dearly beloved, is the day of resurrection and of life. A more delightful rejoicing makes it more welcome after Lent, because days of relaxation have been joined to the time of sadness, so that reward may at once follow patience, according to that [saying]: Those who sow in tears will reap in joy (Ps. 125:5). Whoever of you, then, have sown in tears, take the rewards of exultation. Let each one know that the greater the seeds of weeping he has sown, the greater the fruits of joy he reaps. An image of the future blessings is thus already contained in the present. For just as now there is relaxation after restraint, so in the future there will be rest after labour.

III. Therefore I beseech you, dearly beloved, together with the whole Church, and especially you who, reborn into new salvation, have put on white garments, that you keep the gift you have received pure and spotless, that you preserve the brightness of your dress in your way of life too, and that your hearts be as white as your garments. You heard the evangelist saying today that whoever believe in God are sons of God. For he gave them, he says, power to become sons of God, to those who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God (John 1:12). So you also are not now brought forth from a conception of the flesh, but begotten of God the Father. It remains that you preserve, through the conduct of a holy life, the dignity of your holy origin, and truly, according to what the Apostle says: As newborn infants, desire the rational milk without guile, that by it you may grow to salvation (1 Pet. 2:2). And may the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, guard your hearts and your bodies (Phil. 4:7), through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen.
SERMON V.
On the feast of Saint Paul.
(Delivered at his Church.)

I. A twofold joy of today's festival is renewed for us, dearest brothers, as we celebrate the annual feast of the Teacher of the world. So, exulting in God and offering immense praises to his ineffable majesty, let us rejoice with great gladness; and indeed we ought to be glad with the most abundant delight, because whenever the memory of the saints is celebrated, the minds of the faithful are filled with exceeding joy and are greatly enlightened by spiritual progress, inasmuch as their presence there is not doubted. As we gather, then, dearest ones, in this most sacred hall, we believe that this same excellent preacher stands in our midst and, in a spiritual and in some way invisible manner, rejoices together with us in this his most renowned solemnity. And therefore, dearly beloved, no sloth of sluggishness should entangle any Christian so as to keep him from hastening to this venerable church, where his holy body rests; and especially all those living in the city of Rome and the neighbouring regions, whom it befits above all to make haste. For if all men from the farthest parts of the world, fearing neither the hardship of a most harsh journey nor the long stretches of land, long devoutly to present themselves at the thresholds of the apostles at whatever time they can, what excuse can Roman citizens offer, who, though present on the spot, neglect at least to come together for their feast, while they are known to be guarded by the protecting help of the prayers of these same apostles?

II. For yesterday, the day on which the princes of the apostles themselves were crowned with martyrdom, we hastened with most devoted affection to the church of the blessed apostle Peter and celebrated his solemnity. It was fitting that the feast of the one who merited to obtain the primacy of the apostleship should be celebrated first. But today we keep the birthday of the teacher of the Gentiles and the enlightener of the whole world. For although both alike received the prize of martyrdom, there was reason to transfer the feast of the blessed apostle Paul to this day because of the crowds of people flocking together. As the whole multitude gathered in the hall of blessed Peter, so the same congregation of people, joined together likewise, might flock into the church of his fellow apostle, and the devotion of rejoicing might be in all equally. And see, many, either from sloth or from petty worldly pleasures, have put off coming to this hall of the most excellent blessed Paul. Therefore, dearest brothers, all worldly thought must be cast off and the desires of temporal gain rejected. All of us, hastening with whatever effort we can to celebrate the memory of the saints, above all on the birthday of the blessed Peter and Paul, princes of the apostles, should come together, gathered devoutly alike in the churches of both. As divine favour has distinguished them as equals with the fillet of honours, so let devotion hold them [equal] in their solemnities.

III. For this most blessed man was at first Saul and afterwards Paul; at first, I say, a persecutor, afterwards a preacher. Infected with the savagery of Jewish cruelty, he blazed against the Christians with an excessive madness of ferocity. For as is contained in the Acts of the Apostles, he received power from the chief priests to bring to Jerusalem in chains any worshippers of the Christian religion he could find. He went trembling, seized by great savagery. Suddenly, lit up and terrified by the splendour of a heavenly ray, he heard a voice from heaven saying to him: Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? It is hard for you to kick against the goad (Acts 9:4). At once he fell to the ground and lost the light of his eyes. O kindness of the great mercy of our almighty God! O compassion of inestimable long-suffering! He terrified him a little, so as to console him many times over.
SERMON VI.
On the Annunciation of the blessed Virgin Mary.

Today the Virgin's solemnity calls our tongue to proclamation, brothers, and in the present life it becomes a provider of benefit to those who have come together; and very fittingly. For she is the mother of chastity and the glory of the female sex. That is why she who is a mother in time remains ever a virgin. O how desirable a gathering! For see, both earth and sea offer gifts to the Virgin. The one spreads its back calmly beneath the clouds and pours out rain; the other guides the steps of those who walk upon it without hindrance and bestows gifts from heaven. For natures rejoice and women are honoured, and humanity shines. For where sin abounded, grace also abounded more (Rom. 5:20). Blessed Mary has called us together: the immaculate dew of virginity, the paradise of the rational second Adam, the workshop of the union of natures, the festival of the saving exchange, the bridal chamber in which the Word was wedded to flesh endowed with a soul, the bush of nature which the fire of the divine birth set ablaze [and did not consume]. Truly a light cloud, which carried with a body him at whom the cherubim and seraphim tremble. O heavenly rain! O purest fleece, with which the Shepherd of the sheep clothed himself! Mary, mother and handmaid, virgin and heaven, she alone bearing God and man. Fearful fountain, loom of the dispensation, on which the tunic of the incarnation was woven ineffably; the overseer of this work is the Holy Spirit, and the weaver is the overshadowing power of the Most High; and it clothes the ancient Adam with a flowering garment. This is the holy and immaculate flesh. The shuttle of this loom was admirable grace, and the craftsman, who leapt in through obedience, was the Word of God. For who has seen or who has heard how the uncircumscribed God dwelt in the sacred womb of the holy Virgin, and how he whom heaven does not contain, the womb of the blessed Virgin contained? God was born of a woman, but not bare [God]; and a man, but not mere [man]. And because he was born, taking away the sin of the old man, he showed the gate of salvation. For where the serpent poured out poison through disobedience, there the Word, entering through obedience, fashioned a life-giving temple. From where Cain, the first disciple of sin, emerged, from there Christ, the liberator of our race, sprang up without seed. The lover of all did not blush at a woman's pains, since from there arose the transaction that was being carried out. He was not defiled by dwelling in her whom he himself had formed without dishonour. If the mother did not remain a virgin, then the one born is a mere man, and the birth is no marvel. But if she remained a virgin even after giving birth, then he was born ineffably who entered without hindrance through closed doors, whose union of natures Thomas proclaimed, saying: My Lord and my God (John 20:28). Do not be ashamed, O man; he was made for us the occasion of salvation. If he had not been born of a woman, he would never have died; if he had not died in the flesh, he would never through death have destroyed him who had the power of death, that is, the devil (Heb. 2:14). It is no insult to an architect to stay in what he himself has built. For as clay does not defile the potter who renews what he had fashioned, so it does not defile the undefilable one to come forth from the sacred womb of the Virgin. For he was not defiled when he fashioned her, and passing through her he was not polluted. O womb, in which the bond of our common freedom was drawn up! O belly, in which weapons were forged against death! O threshing floor, on which Christ, the farmer of nature, sprang up like an ear of grain without seed! O temple, in which God became a priest, not changing his nature, but out of mercy putting on him who is according to the order of Melchizedek: for the Word of God was made flesh (John 1:14). Even if the Jews do not believe in the birth, God put on the form of man; even if the pagans disparage the miracle, the judgement of the incarnation is manifest. For this reason it is a scandal to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles (1 Cor. 1:23). The mystery resounds, because the miracle is beyond reason. If the Word had not dwelt in the womb, flesh would never sit upon the throne. If it had been an insult for this reason to enter a womb, it would also be an insult for angels to minister to men. For he who by nature, being God, is impassible, became subject to many sufferings out of mercy. Did Christ then become God by advancement? Far from it. Out of compassion, as we believe, he became man; for we do not proclaim a man made God, but we confess God incarnate. He enrolled his own handmaid as his mother, he who according to his essence is without mother, and according to the dispensation without father. If he is a mere man, he is not without father, for [then] he has a father. But now the very same is without mother as the fashioner, and without father as the one fashioned. Feel shame, O man, at least at the name of the archangel who brought the good news to Mary. He is called Gabriel; and what does Gabriel mean? [The son] of the most blessed virgin, God and man. Therefore, because the one whom he announced was God and man, the name went before, so that the dispensation might be believed. Learn the cause of his coming, and glorify the power of the incarnate one. In this matter the human race owed much, and it fell short of the debt. Through Adam we all signed up to sin, and through him the devil held us as slaves, bringing forward our bonds, only by knowledge of the body (sic). The evil forger of all stood there, shaking the debt against us and demanding judgement. One of two things was therefore necessary: either death should be brought upon all by judgement, because all had sinned, or such a one should be given in compensation as would be the justification of the whole redemption. Now a man could not be saved, for he was subject to the debt. An angel could not redeem, for he fell short of such a liberation. It was necessary only that he who was without sin should die for sinners; for he alone was left for the undoing of the evil. What then? He who changes all nature had led you as God, and he who was lacking in no goodness found for the condemned a most comely life and a most certain release from death, because [he became] man as we are. For speech cannot interpret the miracle. So he who became man dies, and frees what had fallen away, according to Paul, who says: In whom we have redemption through his blood and the forgiveness of sins (Col. 1:14). O astonishing thing! Such a one purchased immortality, for he himself was immortal. For no other such according to the dispensation was, or became, or is, or will be. He alone was born of the Virgin, God and man, possessing a dignity not only able to be set against and to offer a price equal to the multitude of those [to be redeemed], but surpassing all judgements: in that he was Son, preserving what is unchangeable with respect to the Father; in that he was Creator, possessing unfailingly what belongs to power; in his love of showing mercy, displaying without any delay what belongs to compassion; and in that he was priest, offering worthily of faith what served for restoration. Nothing like any of these will anyone find in any other, nor anything near it at any time. For consider his love towards men: was voluntarily condemned, and by being crucified he dissolved the death that existed, and turned the iniquity of those who were killing him into the salvation of the iniquitous. It was not possible, then, for a mere man to save, since he himself needed to be saved, according to Paul, who says: For all have sinned, and need the grace of God (Rom. 3:23). Sin derived from the devil, because the devil was carrying death out to him in great peril, and was cunningly slipping it in among us, and now the undoing of death was impossible. Then those who had been sent by the heavenly physician were accusing it; and so the prophets themselves, seeing that the matter was beyond human skill, cried out to the heavenly physician. And this one said: Lord, bow your heavens and come down (Ps. 143:5). Another: Heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed (Jer. 17:14). Another cried: Stir up your power and come, to set us free (Ps. 79:3). Another said: Alas for me, my soul, for the merciful man has perished from the earth (Mic. 7:1-2). Another: If truly God has dwelt with men (3 Kgs 8:27). Another: Let your mercy quickly take hold of us, Lord (Ps. 78:8). Again another: O God, come to my aid; Lord, make haste to help me (Ps. 69:2). Another: He who is to come will come and will not delay (Hab. 2:3). Another: I have gone astray like a sheep that was lost; seek your servant, Lord (Ps. 118:176). So he who is by nature king and God did not long disregard the oppression of [our] nature. But he came, who was always present, and paid the ransom with his own blood, and gave for the human race, in exchange for death, the body which he had put on from the Virgin, and redeemed the world from the curse of the law, about which Paul also cried: Christ has redeemed us from the curse of the law (Gal. 3:13). For the nature of men, deceived by sin, was in servitude. For he who redeemed us is not a mere man, O Jew, nor yet God unclothed, for he had a body. If he had not put on all these things, he would not have saved me. But he who in the Virgin's womb bore the sentence put on the accused. There that awesome exchange took place: for Christ, giving himself, received flesh, and he the same was with the virgin [and] from the virgin; and this same one overshadowed her, and this one was made flesh from her. If Christ is one and God the Word another, it is no longer a Trinity but a quaternity. Do not tear the tunic of the dispensation, which is woven from above. Do not be a teacher of Arius; that impious man divides the judgement; do not you allow the unity to be torn. For who appeared as man to those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death (Isa. 9:2), and how? Because they were living in darkness, according to Paul, who says: Who has rescued us from the power of darkness (Col. 1:13)? And again: For you were once darkness (Eph. 5:8). Who then shone forth? Let David teach you, saying: Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord (Ps. 117:26). Who is this? Say it openly, O David: God [is] the Lord, and he has shone upon us (Ps. 117:27). The natures came together, and the unity remained unconfused. He came to save, but he also had to suffer. For how could a mere man do both? He could not prevail to save; and God unclothed could not suffer. He, being God by nature, became man, and what he had purchased he saved, and what he became he endured. Therefore, when the synagogue had crowned him with thorns, holy Church said, weeping: Daughters of Jerusalem, go out and see the crown with which his mother crowned him (Song 3:11). For he bore a crown of thorns, to dissolve the sentence of thorns; he [was] in the bosom of the Father and in the womb of the Virgin, in his mother's arms and upon the wings of the winds; above he was adored by angels, and below he reclined with tax-collectors. The Seraphim did not advance, and Pilate was questioning [him]. A slave was striking [him], and creation was terrified. He was being nailed on the cross, and he was on the throne. He was lying in the tomb, and stretching out the heaven like a skin (Ps. 103:2). He was counted among the dead, and hell was being despoiled. Below they slandered him as a deceiver, and above he was glorified by the saints. O astonishing mystery! I see the miracles, and I proclaim the Godhead; I behold the passion, and I do not deny the humanity. But Emmanuel appeared by nature as man, yet as God he did not break the virginal enclosure, but came forth from the womb in the same way as he entered through hearing. He was born in the same way as he was conceived. He entered without suffering, he came forth without corruption, according to the prophet Ezekiel, who says: God turned me, he says, to the way of the outer gate of the sanctuary, which faces the East; and it was shut; and the Lord said to me: Son of man, this gate shall be shut and shall not be opened (Ezek. 44:1-2). No one has passed through it, but the Lord God alone will go in and come out; and the gate will be shut. See the manifest proof concerning the holy Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary. Let every contradiction henceforth be dissolved, and let the teaching of the holy Scriptures be made bright, that we may obtain the kingdom of heaven in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be honour and glory together with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, through the never-ending ages of ages. Amen.
SERMON VII.
On Saint Dionysius the Martyr.

I. Divine kindness has deigned, dearly beloved brothers, to renew for us today the holy and glorious feast, worthy of all veneration, of our most blessed Father and pastor, the most holy Dionysius. We believe that it is proclaimed in heaven no less, while it is devoutly venerated on earth even by us sinners; for although the mind of Christians shares in all the solemnities of the saints, yet we must rejoice in a proper and more particular way in the feast of our leader and Father, so that where the outstanding death of the martyr and bishop was glorified, there on the day of his martyrdom joy may hold first place. Yet whatever service we pay him, let it be referred to the praise of his Creator and ours. For, as your devout presence itself testifies, brothers, you understand that the return of this day concerns our common joy, since you run together to the pastor's yearly feast to celebrate his honour; for we believe that you draw near to the divine mercy with more abundant devotion through the prayers of the present father, since you gather with careful zeal for his holy vigils; for he whose reverence has gathered you does not forsake your devotion. Indeed, brothers, like a loving father he rejoices in your holy services, and exults in the number of his sons.

II. O feast of our holy Father, venerable to us! O truly blessed solemnity, to be preferred with great praises, at which the angels praise the Lord in the stars! The assemblies of priests resound with great honour, and the choir of martyrs proclaims the palm of victory; at which mouths long closed are unlocked on earth, the blinded eyes of the blind return [to sight], while the dread stains of sins are washed away, and the prayers of all are taken up as the deeds of the devout. For although, dearest brothers, when the circuit of the year has come round, his sacred vigils seem to be renewed for us, and they are new and astonishing for Christian peoples over the spaces of time, yet to the glory of Christ they remain with us daily, praiseworthy for their miracles. For what sick man, coming here, will not go away healthy? Who, weighed down by the burden of his offences, will have said with a groan that he is guilty, and not win forgiveness? Surely, as I believe, the prophet had foreseen the feast of this day long before, when he said to the Lord: Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house, and the place of the dwelling of your glory (Ps. 25:8). And, proclaiming worthily the sacred passing of our most blessed Father, and praising the Lord, he said: Blessed is he whom you have chosen and taken up, Lord; he shall dwell in your courts (Ps. 64:5).

III. For great and wonderful, dearly beloved, is the gift which the divine favour granted to this man after the apostles; in granting him the authority of its power, it declared what glory he had with it. This, my brothers, this is wholly that blessed and truly praiseworthy priest and martyr of Christ, Dionysius the Areopagite, whom the Acts of the Apostles mention: a citizen of the Athenians, sprung from noble stock, instructed from infancy in the rudiments of dialectic and rhetorical studies, born on the island of Diona in the province of Attica. He was called the Areopagite because he had been educated in the liberal arts in the place called the Areopagus, and had not only learned the same school of thought of that people, but was the most learned teacher of others. But, with the help of the mercy of him who deigned to promise through the prophet, saying: Open your mouth and I will fill it (Ps. 80:11), and who willed the mouth of a brute animal to be loosed, I have thought it right to make known to you a few of the signs of this saint, which we believe will without doubt please your devout minds. For some things we learned by reading in certain Greek books, and some are known to us from the account of faithful men.

IV. In the name of God, Eugippius the *aristarcus* [chief scholar] to Onesiphorus the *primicerius* [head of an office], greeting. We have received the letters of your charity, brought by Anatolius, in which it was set down that we should take care, with literary zeal, to write back to you what is known to our memory, or recalled from the ancient tradition of those of old, about the various doctrines or the variety of the sects of the Athenians, or about the site or layout of the city of Athens. And among other things we found in your writings [a request] that I should set out for you in a brief style the things done in the city of the Athenians itself in the times of the apostles, and how, when the apostle Paul came there, certain men resisted him with empty philosophies and false imaginings of things. Indeed you also asked of us that, concerning Symmachus and Apollinaris the Chronopagite, and also Dionysius the Areopagite, who as hearers of the apostle Paul were renowned at Athens in [those] times, I should set out for you more clearly what I knew of them, and from what lineage of the Athenians and from what stock they sprang. This, according to the weakness of our wit, as we have been able to hear it through past times by the tradition of antiquity, we have sent to you by Anatolius, our son and the bearer of your letter.

V. The city of Athens, set on the border of Thrace and of the Lacedaemonians, mountainous in the lie of its lands, shut in by the straits of the Ionian Sea and bounded on the left side by the Aegean Sea, was a famous and ancient city, rich in the fertility of its lands, the nurse of eloquence and the mother of philosophers and wise men, and it excelled other cities in the wealth of its various arts and riches. It is set in the province of Attica, where Cecrops and Minander were renowned as kings of the peoples; where Apollo, and Hippocrates, and Aristotle were born, who shone over the whole world in those times with the flowers of wisdom. At this time Cecrops and Minander the kings were worshippers of images, for the superstitious religion of idols was first found among them and burst forth. It is described as divided into five regions. The first region is the one that faces the Aegean Sea, a hill rising above the city, where golden images of Saturn and Priapus are hidden by various illusions; this region the Greeks call the Chronopagium, for the Greeks call Saturn Chronos. The second region of Athens is the one that faces towards Chios, where there was a terebinth of wonderful size, and where fauns, rustic men, were worshipped by shepherds on appointed days. The third region of the city of Athens is the one that faces the harbour of Neptune, where they worshipped an image of Diana and of Aegean Neptune. This place the pagans call Popedon, for the Greeks call Neptune Popedon. The fourth region of the Athenian city is where the idol of Mars and the image of Hercules were set up, which is on the hill of Tritonia: a hill set in the middle of the city, where the throng of the whole people came at the new moon, namely to worship Mars and Hercules, whom they adored as the mightiest gods; this place the Greeks call the Ariopagium, for Ares is said in Greek, Mars in Latin. The fifth region of the Athenian city is the one that faces the Sichaean gate, where an idol and image of Mercury was set up; this place is named Ermipagos, for Mercury is called Hermes in Greek. This city flourished as the most noble above the other Greek cities in the wealth of sea and land, of woods and mountains, of rivers and green places; and it, which was then preferred as head to the other cities, is now brought low, crushed and cut off by the onslaught of the nations.

VI. Apollo was so called, being descended from the lineage of a certain Apollinis, a most noble prince of the Athenians; his father was Nicolaus, a man of great ability, a citizen strong in the study of letters and a famous master of the Argolic art. While his son Apollo was held renowned among the schools of the philosophers, and was turning over the authoritative libraries, and while he was given over to philosophy and empty superstitions, he heard the apostle Paul preaching new doctrines unheard of before. And when he could not resist him, he found that the teaching which Paul taught at Athens was true. So, leaving the empty superstitions of the Gentiles, he threw himself at the Apostle's feet and begged him to show him the true teaching and the way of salvation, and he said that he was now a disciple of Christ, not of Saturn.

VII. When these things had been done, and Paul one day had seen the Areopagus, he began to ask blessed Dionysius what he worshipped, or what deities he served in so spacious and venerable a place. Dionysius said to him: The gods whom our fathers worshipped, by whose power and skill mother earth is held together, these we worship, and we adore the altars which are consecrated in the name and honour of Mars and Hercules, of Mercury and Priapus. But while Paul was surveying the several altars and images of the false gods, among the other altars he found one altar on which was written above: To the unknown god (Acts 17:23). And Paul, turning to him and to the rest who were accompanying him, asked them who that unknown god was. Dionysius answered him among the others, saying: That god has not yet been shown among the gods, but he is unknown to us, and will be in the age to come; and he is the God who is to reign in heaven and on earth, and his kingdom will have no end. Paul asked again: What do you think? Will he be a man or a spirit of the gods? In answer they said: That he is both true God and true man, and he is to renew the world; but he is still unknown to men, because his dwelling is with the gods in heaven. Paul said: That God I preach to you whom until now you have held unknown. For, born of a virgin, he sits at the right hand of the Father, true God and true man, through whom all things were made. God is known in Judaea, and his holy name in Israel (Ps. 75:2). Him whom you have held unknown until now, know now, for he alone is God, and besides him there is no other God, who has led you back from death to life, who has joined heaven and earth, men and angels in the unity of his kingdom, who gives life and puts to death (1 Kgs 2:6); who shuts and no one opens; who opens and no one shuts (Rev. 3:7).

VIII. As Paul preached these and very many other things, while he preached in the several temples that Christ is the Son of God, Dionysius, receiving the true teaching and the doctrine of salvation, and recognising that the idols he served were nothing, and were demons rather than gods, and clearly perceiving the Holy Spirit too and the words of life in Paul's teaching, spurred by divine grace, turned to Paul and asked him to pray to the divine mercy for him, so that he might be worthy to be his disciple. And when Paul was making a journey on the next day, a certain blind man, deprived of the light of his eyes, asked to be healed by Paul's power. At once, therefore, the holy apostle, made an imitator of his Lord and master Jesus Christ, placed his cross on the eyes long closed, saying: May Christ, namely our Lord and master, who put clay on the eyes of the man born blind, and he was at once found worthy to receive light, himself restore light to your eyes by his power. Then in wonderful fashion the man born blind was found worthy to receive light in his eyes, and Paul at once addressed him with these words, saying: Go to Dionysius, and tell him that Paul, servant of Christ Jesus, has sent me to you, that, mindful of your promise, you may not be slow to come to him, so that, receiving the baptism of salvation, you may be released from all the bonds of your offences. At once the man who had received light fulfilled the words of the one commanding with the foot of obedience, and hastening to Dionysius, reported Paul's words to him in order. But Dionysius, already the Lord's chosen one, when he saw the blind man walking with sound eyes, addressed him with these words, saying: Are you the one whom all your kinsmen knew as born blind? He answered him: I am indeed the one who was born blind, and to whom until now the light of this present life was denied. But Paul himself, who bade you come to him, calling on the power of Jesus Christ his master, has granted me the light of health. Then at once rising, he hastens to the bidding of the command of blessed Paul. Why do I delay longer? He believed forthwith, and sprinkled with the water of holy baptism, having renounced the errors of the pagans, he gave himself over to be instructed by his teaching; and then, at Paul's own command, he preached the Gospel of Christ. Converting many from Thessalonica to the way of salvation, he converted the greatest part of that province to the faith.

IX. They say too that this most blessed man, kindled by the ardour of the Holy Spirit, when the Lord of the world hung fastened on the cross by the hands of the Jews, and the sun, dreading the death of its Lord, changed the rays of its light into the horror of foul night, and had covered the regions of the world with a night of darkness, said: This night, which we marvel to see come down new upon our eyes, has shown that the salvation of the whole world has come. O truly holy seer! O man truly steeped in divine light, who was already so chosen beforehand by a blessed lot that one not yet reborn from the sacred font, still a pagan in his members, had the power to be the reporter of so great a mystery! For since he excelled in the grace of so many gifts, he shone in every way in the eloquence of his teaching and in the flowers of the Scriptures. The Greeks indeed relate that he wrote three marvellous books: one which is called Antiheresis, that is, a volume against all heresies; one on Contempt of the World and the Nine Orders of Angels; one which, as we have heard, is kept in the archives of Constantinople. This holy man too blessed Gregory in his homilies praises with all veneration as a true and ancient Father.

X. But how, under Domitian, the persecutor of Christians, he passed through the glory of martyrdom to those above, the light of his passion has made known to you. We, however, out of the weakness of our wit and our sluggish learning, not so much rashly as with a happy presumption, for love and reverence of our most holy lord and patron, have briefly made this known to your charity for the sake of edification, knowing this: that if we have rendered you any service, you will without doubt help us with your prayers before the holy martyr. I think it worthwhile too that, amid the solemnity of so great a patron, priest and martyr, the memory of the blessed Rusticus and Eleutherius also be recited, so that where on one day they underwent martyrdom for Christ, there on the day of their martyrdom there may be a festival worthy of veneration. For while we must rejoice in the commemoration of all the holy martyrs, yet in the excellence of these martyrs we must rightly glory more exultantly, whom the grace of God raised to so high a summit among all the members of the Church that Christ's grace and election had made them peers, their labour alike, and their end equal.

XI. For these are the holy men, your fathers, through whom, Gaul, the Gospel of Christ and the grace of salvation shone upon you, and you who were the mother of error were made the daughter of truth. These are your holy fathers and true shepherds, who handed you over to be fitted for the heavenly kingdom. For although, enlarged by many victories, you have extended the rule of your kingdom over land and sea, yet what the labour of war brought you is less than what Christian peace subdued through the mouths of these precious martyrs. For, not knowing the author of your dignity, while you seemed to lord it over the other nations, you were in fact subdued and serving great errors. For the more tightly you were bound by the devil, the more wonderfully you have been set free through their sufferings. Happy are you, Gaul, who were found worthy to receive priests so great and of such a kind. Happy are you, Paris, whose soil was found worthy to be watered with the blood of such great martyrs. Behold, you are mighty in the glory of three martyrs; behold, with their gleaming ranks their blessed rewards have encircled you, and have crowned you as with a diadem set with the honour of many gems. Under their protection, dearly beloved brothers, with our minds prepared for an example of patience and for the strengthening of faith, let us imitate their examples as far as we can, so that the merits of the flock may arrive where the fortitude of the shepherds has gone before. For this, dearest brothers, we must greatly take care: that while we are honoured by the present festivals of the martyrs, we may be able to be joined to their holy fellowship in the future. See, my brothers, as you behold, the bodies of the blessed martyrs are covered with an abundance of gold and gems, and those who here for Christ bowed their happy necks to the impious, the princes of the earth worship with bowed necks. How great, then, do you think is the glory with which they are exalted there among the choirs of angels and archangels, when here their blessed corpses are extolled with such honours?

XII. These things, brothers and lords, as we said above, we have taken care to make known to your ears for the solemnity of this great day, not so much rashly as with happy devotion, knowing that a devotion, though unlearned, yet pure, and a faithful love, have the reward of a just recompense, as we too have experienced before and our elders have proved. And we believe and trust that amid all the labours of this life we shall always be helped by the prayers of these our special patrons to obtain the mercy of God, so that as much as we are weighed down by our own sins, so much may we be lifted up by their holy merits. And we who are wasted away in our iniquities, may we be cherished by the prayers of our blessed fathers the martyrs, by the grant of the very Son of the eternal Father, who with him and the Holy Spirit lives, rules and reigns, now and through the immortal ages of ages. Amen.
SERMON VIII.
On Absalom: how he persecuted his father.

I. Absalom, most wicked, lost his mind, lost his sense, let go of counsel; he hounds his father, puts the innocent to flight; he pursues his begetter, usurps the rule, seizes power, invades the kingdom, not to enter into a partnership of the kingdom with his father, but to possess the whole kingdom by his father's blood. Absalom lost counsel, I say, when he desired to earn rule by parricide; he let go of sense when he longed to gain the kingdom through his father's destruction. He hurries, he hastens, he seeks to crush the innocent, he who, guilty, was to die while his father survived. But David, on the other hand, humble and mild, gives way to the man, flees the pursuer, avoids the enemy, sets aside his feelings, lest either the death of the parricide bring him grief, or his own slaying show his son guilty. He wishes to check his son's fury by fleeing; he longs to soften the parricide's savagery by avoiding him. But the cruelty conceived in the mind could not be calmed, so far had monstrous savagery incited it to carry out the crime. O innocence, how much danger you undergo among the guilty, how much trouble you meet through the wicked! Most holy David offended so many maddened armies because he did not forsake [them]; he met the rage of so many peoples because he did not harm [them]. Absalom alone is guilty and unhappy, and a whole army breathes against the father. The deadly hands of many are armed for the slaughter of the father; they are roused to avenge another's crime upon an innocent man; the fury of one parricide drives so many thousands mad; the madness of one has made many mad.

II. For David offended his son because he would not avenge on him the murder of his brother. For crimes always grow while they are not cut back, and one leaps on to the increase of misdeeds whenever sin is soothed by impunity. For while in Absalom the crime of the slain brother is not punished, the crime relapses and is repeated in the parricide of the father. You, you, I say, unhappy armies, I admonish; you I exhort with the affection of piety: why do you rush into another's crime? Why do you aid the madness of a raging man? Why do you show yourselves like the parricide, and mad? Desert, I beg, desert the guilty man, desert one who is to die by a new punishment. For perhaps if you desert him, he will stop, whom your number provoked to dare. Surely let him alone perish who wars down the force of nature; let him alone fall who attacks a father's love. For either he will stop, repenting, or he will persist and perish. For I grieve for the guilty man, I grieve for the impious one, I grieve for one who is to die by a new punishment. Who taught you to leap into this crime, most foul parricide? What fury provoked you to dare so monstrous a crime? If he offended, he is your father; if he harmed you, he is your begetter; nay rather, he neither offended nor harmed you. Let filial love conquer fury, let affection overcome madness, let nature war down cruelty. Or did your father offend you because he did not harm you, or did he offend you for this reason, that he did not harm you, who perhaps would not have offended had he harmed you? Give back your affection, show filial love; you spare yourself when you turn your hands away from your father, whom you ought to defend if you had known another to dare what you dare. Where now will fathers find comfort, where will parents find protection, if they find their sons parricides? Or when are outside things safe, if those of our own household stand against us? Beasts and dumb cattle keep the laws of natural love, and those to whom nature denies reason it does not, however, deny love. To kill an innocent man is an abomination, to kill a father a crime, to cut the throat of a prophet a deed unheard of and unknown to all mortals before this time. But cease now from this crime, cease, lest all good men always shudder at you, lest the bold learn from you what they did not know; cease, I say, lest whoever after you commits so great a crime use you as his precedent. Why do you hand on a new crime to the world? Why do you teach what the nature of filial love did not know? Why do you desire what love itself shudders at? Why do you dare to accomplish what the Lord will be compelled to punish with a new punishment?

III. Meanwhile the parricide's fury is not lessened, not reined in; it blazes, and, monstrous, is kindled for the worse. He desires to fulfil the crime he conceived, he longs to carry out most urgently the wickedness he has planned. To one committing an abomination all things are slow; to one hastening to crime, the arrangements seem to delay. He desires to complete the parricide before he acts; he hurries to make away with his father before he kills him; he thirsts for his father's blood, he craves the gore of his begetter; he fears to delay even a little, lest either his anger, delayed, should fail, or his frenzy, postponed, should grow faint. Battle is arrayed nearby, the line is drawn up, the fight is prepared, kindred forces blaze against one another. On one side the parricide inflames the army against his father; on the other David entreats the departing commanders that the son be spared: Spare, he says, my son Absalom. On one side madness rises against the begetter, on the other clemency begs that the parricide be spared; on one side fury, on the other love is at work; on one side insanity, on the other mercy is set forth; on one side cruelty, on the other goodness is shown. The parricide, unharmed, rages; David is harmed and grows gentle; love is warred down by impiety; yet the father's love is not moved, nor conquered by the sword, nor changed by terror; the parricide is neither broken by reason nor deterred by imminent death. He is hardened toward punishment, he is driven to his penalty, nor does he any longer deserve salvation in anything, who tries to rob his father of his life.

IV. Look back now, most wicked enemy; abominable man, look back now, parricide. Look back, I say: everything everywhere, as it were, is turned against you. Look back: the very nature of things fights against you. And although heaven contends against you, the earth is moved, and an army fights, yet another war, unknown to you and unexpected, awaits you. Another battle is already prepared for you, one to catch you as you flee, to destroy you as you commit your crime, to kill you as you hasten. For it is not these armies of flesh that you see, whom either your fury armed against your father or your father's need roused against you. Though they rightly draw their swords against you, brandish their blades and hurl their lances, so that the grief of the injured father may be washed away by your death, yet a tree will catch you as you flee, its branches will destroy you, its timbers will hang you. There is at hand, I say, a tree that did not heed the father, that you should be spared, and strives to fulfil the commands of God; nor will you be able to escape this war unpunished, you who tried to inflict death on your begetter. So, when battle is joined, the enemies are laid low, the adversaries fall, the foes are conquered, the enemy is stripped bare, the parricide is deserted. Now he perceives his own punishment in [the fate of] his men; now he recognizes in the destruction of his own the penalty due to him; now he fears, now he dreads, now he ponders his own death. At last he seeks a beast, mounts a mule, flings himself into headlong flight, and hastens to the tree prepared nearby, to which he is handed over. Driven by a violent impact, with [the mule] drawn from under him and running off beneath into the fields, he is thrust among the branches, bound fast by the timbers, held fast and hanging with his throat pierced. Now he is found dead by all, he whom heaven could no longer look upon alive, nor the earth bear any further.

V. O the abominable deserts of the parricide! The wrong done to the father is avenged not by the sword of one fighting, not by an enemy's hand, not by the stroke of one hurling a spear; but timbers vindicate it, a tree avenges it, branches defend it. Nor is there any creature that was not moved when it perceived that the Lord himself, its maker, was moved. So all return from the war, the parricide, the author of the war, laid low, by whose blood the crime is washed away, by whose punishment the monstrous cruelty is buried. All rejoice, all are glad; David alone mourns his son, laments the death of the parricide. Why do you mourn, glorious father? Why by lamenting do you seem to approve what Absalom dared? Why do you weep for the wicked man, as though you had wished him to commit parricide? The glory of the victorious army is broken, and the enemy's death is even wept for, nor can there be joy in victory while the parricide's punishment is mourned. He was not your son, who so violated a father's feelings. He did not deserve to be called yours, who violated the right of a most exalted father. It was not the armies that disregarded you, nor the commanders to whom you gave orders on behalf of so wicked a man, but that tree: it avenged you, it defended you, it vindicated the wrong done to the injured father, though it had not heard you. Your vindication has brought security to fathers and removed the boldness of parricides; through you the wrong done to nature has been avenged, and fatherly love restored. For he had to perish by a new punishment, who wished to bring upon the world a new crime, the destruction of a father.
